wstep: This card describes mango leather following the NCHFP recipe: mango purée with honey and spices is dried in a dehydrator at 140 °F (60 °C) for about 10 hours. [T:SUS-030,SUS-217]

akapity: NCHFP does not describe aam papad: this card is the NCHFP mango leather recipe, not traditional aam papad; it does not cover papaya. [T:SUS-216]
4 cups mango purée (from about 4 large, unripe mangoes), 1 cup clover honey, 1/2 teaspoon ground cinnamon, 1/4 teaspoon ground nutmeg and 1/4 teaspoon ground cloves. [T:SUS-216]
This makes about 2 dryer trays 14 inches (about 36 cm) in diameter, or 8 fruit rolls. [T:SUS-216]
You may omit the honey (unsweetened leather); for a lighter colour add 1/4 teaspoon (750 mg) of ascorbic acid to the purée with the spices. [T:SUS-221]
Preheat the dehydrator to 140 °F (60 °C). [T:SUS-217]
Wash, peel and chop the mangoes and purée until smooth; pass the purée through a food mill or sieve, discard the coarse fibre and mix in the honey and spices thoroughly. [T:SUS-217]
Lightly spray two dehydrator fruit roll liners with vegetable oil cooking spray and spread the purée evenly 1/4 inch (about 6 mm) thick. [T:SUS-217,SUS-030]
Do not use trays or screens made of galvanized mesh; also avoid copper and aluminium mesh. [T:SUS-008]
Dry continuously for about 10 hours with the air temperature held steadily at 140 °F (60 °C); check it periodically with a thermometer. [T:SUS-030,SUS-217]
The leather is ready when there are no sticky areas and touching gently in several places near the centre leaves no indentation; the time depends strongly on the humidity of the room. [T:SUS-217]
An electric dehydrator gives the most reliable results; an oven is suitable only if it can hold 140–145 °F (about 60–63 °C). [T:SUS-220]
Line a cookie sheet with edges with plastic wrap, smoothing out the wrinkles, or spray it with vegetable oil; do not use waxed paper or aluminium foil. [T:SUS-220,SUS-212]

Leave the oven door open 2–6 inches (about 5–15 cm) and keep the air temperature at about 140 °F (60 °C), checking it with a thermometer; if it gets too high, turn the oven off for a while. [T:SUS-220]
Begin checking a large leather at 8–10 hours. [T:SUS-220]
Peel the leather from the liners while still warm; if it cools too much, re-warm it slightly in the dehydrator. [T:SUS-218]
Cut it into quarters, lay it on plastic food wrap 1–2 inches (about 2.5–5 cm) longer at each end and roll it up; when cool, twist the ends of the wrap tightly. [T:SUS-218]
Pack only completely cooled rolls: warm dried food sweats, and that moisture can be enough for mould to grow. [T:SUS-024]
Store the rolls short term, up to about 1 month, in freezer-quality zippered plastic bags or airtight plastic containers, in a cool, dark, dry place. [T:SUS-219,SUS-066]
For storage up to 1 year, keep tightly wrapped rolls in the freezer. [T:SUS-028]
Store the dried fruit in clean, dry canning jars, plastic freezer containers with tight-fitting lids or plastic freezer bags. [T:SUS-064]
Packaging must be food grade: do not use trash bags or plastic or fibreboard containers that previously held non-food items. [T:SUS-065]
Pack amounts that can be used at one time: each opening exposes the dried fruit to air and moisture, which lowers quality and can lead to spoilage. [T:SUS-067]
Vacuum packaging is not a preservation method by itself: removing oxygen increases the risk of botulism, and a product that needs refrigeration still needs it. [T:SUS-025]
Check the dried fruit often (glass shows condensation); if it has taken up moisture but is not spoiled, use it at once or dry it again and repack it. [T:SUS-023]
Throw away mouldy dried fruit; also throw away dried fruit that smells off. [T:SUS-022]
